title: AI is driving a flood of crypto bug reports. Now it’s helping sort them
summary: Bug bounty platform HackerOne said it’s increasing its triage throughput with AI agents after a record quarter of reports in the third quarter.
content: Bug bounty platform HackerOne is using AI agents to increase its triage throughput for vulnerability reports. The platform experienced a record-breaking quarter for reports in the third quarter, largely driven by artificial intelligence. To manage the massive influx of security submissions, HackerOne is now deploying AI technology to help sort and process the reports efficiently.

title: Ethereum’s Co-Founder Takes On Crypto’s Next Security Threat. Who Is Vitalik Buterin?
summary: Key takeaways Vitalik Buterin’s November 26 essay argues that crypto security must extend to the physical chips inside devices, summed up as “Not your silicon, not your keys.” He wants manufacturers to publish physical chip layouts (GDS files) so investigators can compare real hardware against the design. Researcher Andrew Huang’s infrared inspection technique (IRIS) can examine chips without removing them, but it has resolution limits and is not a universal fix. The essay is a proposal, not a claim that existing hardware wallets are compromised, and publishing it does not give Buterin power to change Ethereum unilaterally. Arkham attributes about $390 million in assets to Buterin, mostly roughly 224,000 ETH, though his true net worth is not publicly established. Who is Vitalik Buterin, and why is Ethereum’s co-founder now questioning the security of the very devices crypto investors use to protect their wealth? The 32-year-old programmer has turned his attention to a problem that even open-source software cannot necessarily solve: compromised computer chips. In an essay published on November 26, Buterin argued that cryptocurrency security needs to extend beyond software and into the physical hardware on which it runs. His message builds on one of crypto’s oldest principles, but with a new twist: “ Not your silicon, not your keys. Vitalik Buterin · Essay, November 26 For someone who helped build an alternative to centralized financial infrastructure, questioning the manufacturers behind that infrastructure seems like a natural next step. It also reflects a security philosophy that has become increasingly visible in Buterin’s work, from his push for greater privacy and quantum safety on Ethereum’s roadmap to his interest in independently verifiable computing. Who Is Vitalik Buterin? Vitalik Buterin is a Russian-Canadian programmer, researcher and writer who conceived Ethereum in 2013, at the age of 19. Born in Russia in 1994 and raised in Canada, Buterin discovered Bitcoin in 2011. He went on to co-found Bitcoin Magazine, where he explored the technology and economics behind cryptocurrencies long before digital assets attracted mainstream financial institutions. His involvement in Bitcoin exposed him to a problem that would eventually lead to Ethereum. Blockchain technology had potential beyond transferring money, but building more sophisticated applications on Bitcoin presented technical limitations. Rather than trying to accommodate every possible application within Bitcoin’s existing architecture, Buterin began working on a blockchain designed specifically for programmability. At the time, he was studying computer science at the University of Waterloo, where he also worked as a research assistant to cryptographer Ian Goldberg. According to the University of Waterloo, Buterin received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship in 2014 and subsequently left university to work on Ethereum full-time. How Vitalik Buterin Created Ethereum In November 2013, Buterin wrote the initial draft of what would become the Ethereum whitepaper. The proposal described a blockchain with a general-purpose programming environment. Developers would no longer need to create an entirely new network every time they wanted to build a decentralized application. Consider a lending platform. Instead of relying on a bank to manage collateral, calculate interest and authorize withdrawals, developers could encode those rules into smart contracts running on Ethereum. That does not eliminate every risk. Smart contracts can contain bugs, depend on unreliable external data or operate under centralized administrative controls. What Ethereum introduced was the ability to execute financial and other programmable agreements on a shared blockchain. Although Buterin originated the concept, Ethereum was not built by him alone. Its founding team included seven other individuals: Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, Charles Hoskinson, Anthony Di Iorio, Mihai Alisie, Jeffrey Wilcke and Amir Chetrit. The project’s first live network, known as Frontier, launched on July 30, 2015. What began as an experimental computing platform eventually became the foundation for much of the decentralized finance industry. Stablecoins, decentralized exchanges, lending protocols and tokenized financial assets now use the infrastructure that Buterin and Ethereum’s early contributors helped establish. The network’s own evolution, particularly its transition to proof-of-stake and the development of Layer 2 scaling networks, has shaped Ethereum’s first decade. Vitalik Buterin’s Latest Warning: Can Crypto Wallets Really Be Trusted? A hardware wallet is supposed to keep private keys away from potentially compromised computers and smartphones. But what happens if the device itself cannot be trusted? Buterin’s latest research examines that possibility. He points to supply chain attacks involving tampered wallets and considers the potential for malicious modifications concealed inside apparently legitimate chips. Open-source firmware allows researchers to examine the instructions a device runs. But those instructions reveal little about whether the manufactured chip has been altered. Buterin wants manufacturers to disclose physical chip layouts, known as GDS files, so investigators have a reference against which to inspect actual hardware. The distinction matters. Knowing what a chip is designed to do is not necessarily the same as knowing what the chip inside your wallet actually does. The Technology That Could Help Detect Compromised Chips One approach highlighted by Buterin comes from hardware security researcher Andrew Huang, better known as bunnie. Huang has been developing a technique called Infra-Red, In Situ inspection (IRIS), which exploits the fact that silicon becomes transparent at certain infrared wavelengths. Using infrared illumination and suitable imaging equipment, researchers can examine parts of a chip’s internal structure without necessarily removing it from its circuit board. The technique could help detect substituted components or unexpected differences between manufactured chips and their intended designs. However, it is not a universal solution. In a 2024 update on his research, Huang explained that infrared imaging has resolution limits. It cannot reliably reveal every microscopic feature of modern chips. Combining imaging with additional electrical testing could improve confidence in a component’s integrity. That is an important limitation for crypto investors. Publishing an open hardware design does not automatically make a wallet secure, just as publishing a smart contract’s code does not establish that it is free of vulnerabilities. Buterin acknowledges that sophisticated hardware inspections are more likely to be performed by specialist organizations than ordinary wallet owners. His essay is a proposal for improving security, not an announcement that existing hardware wallets have all been compromised. Does Vitalik Buterin Control Ethereum? Despite his status as Ethereum’s most recognizable co-founder, Buterin is not its CEO. Ethereum is maintained through the participation of independent developers, researchers, node operators, validators and other ecosystem contributors. Changes to the network involve technical proposals, discussion, software development and adoption by participants. Buterin has considerable influence over those discussions, but publishing a proposal does not give him the authority to implement it unilaterally. His role within the Ethereum Foundation is also distinct from control over the blockchain itself. In its April 2025 governance announcement, the Foundation described Buterin’s responsibilities as providing technical and intellectual guidance to the wider ecosystem. His research can influence the direction Ethereum takes. Whether the network ultimately follows that direction depends on considerably more than his endorsement. How Much Is Vitalik Buterin Worth? Buterin accumulated considerable wealth through his involvement in Ethereum, with much of his publicly visible cryptocurrency wealth tied to ETH. However, his exact net worth is not publicly established. Blockchain analytics can estimate the value of assets held in wallets attributed to him, but those figures do not necessarily account for all his investments, liabilities, private assets or holdings at addresses that have not been publicly identified. They also fluctuate with cryptocurrency prices. A wallet valuation should therefore not be confused with a complete assessment of his personal wealth. What Is Vitalik Buterin’s Vision for the Future of Crypto? Buterin’s latest essay is part of a longer-running interest in making digital infrastructure independently verifiable. In September 2025, he published The Importance of Full-Stack Openness and Verifiability, exploring how transparency could extend across the hardware and software underpinning increasingly important parts of people’s lives. His broader research includes cryptography, privacy, blockchain scalability and Ethereum’s transition toward greater quantum resistance. Buterin has previously called for greater experimentation across Ethereum’s application layer without compromising its core principles of censorship resistance, open-source development, privacy and security. These interests share a practical concern: whether users can independently establish that the systems they rely on behave as intended. There is a commercial obstacle, though. Semiconductor manufacturers invest heavily in proprietary processes, and designing chips specifically for inspectability can involve performance compromises. But a device signing a cryptocurrency transaction does not necessarily need the computing power of a modern AI processor. That makes security-focused hardware a potentially useful starting point. More than a decade ago, Buterin challenged the idea that blockchains should primarily be used to transfer money. His latest work challenges another assumption the industry has grown comfortable with: that trusting the code is enough. For crypto investors, the next meaningful development may come from hardware manufacturers willing to make their products independently inspectable, rather than another software update promising greater security.

While hardware inspection tools like IRIS have limits, Buterin's proposal highlights growing concerns over supply chain security in the crypto industry.

title: Zcash Developers Race to Secure Crypto. Can Quantum Computing Break Bitcoin?
summary: Key takeaways Zcash development team Zakura (November 26) called for accelerated retirement of the older Sapling privacy pool, which it estimated held about 400,000 ZEC. A November 27 dashboard snapshot showed about 306,684 ZEC still in Sapling, though that does not prove the warning prompted anyone to move funds. Zakura’s concern is speculative, unverified mathematical advances, not a successful quantum attack, and Shielded Labs expects to pick a post-quantum direction by the end of January 2027. The Quantum Ledger counts about 7.23 million BTC (35.9% of issued supply) with public keys already visible on-chain; Glassnode’s May estimate was 6.04 million BTC. No reliable date exists for a quantum computer that can break crypto signatures, but upgrading blockchains, wallets and custody could itself take years. Can quantum computing break crypto? For years, the question has largely been treated as a problem for the distant future. Zcash developers, however, are already discussing what to do with hundreds of thousands of coins that could become vulnerable if certain cryptographic protections fail. On November 26, Zcash development team Zakura called for the accelerated retirement of Sapling, an older privacy system that the team estimated still held around 400,000 ZEC. The recommendation followed speculation about mathematical breakthroughs at artificial intelligence laboratories. A day earlier, Shielded Labs published its first technical update on a separate project designed to protect Zcash against future quantum computers. Neither development means cryptocurrency has been cracked. Together, however, they raise a more pressing question: can blockchain developers replace the mathematics protecting investors’ money before someone finds a way around it? What Is Quantum Computing? Quantum computing is a way of processing information using the properties of quantum mechanics. Unlike conventional computers, which represent information using bits with a value of either zero or one, quantum computers operate using quantum bits, commonly known as qubits. By manipulating these qubits, researchers can design algorithms capable of solving certain mathematical problems far more efficiently than conventional computers. The important word here is certain. A quantum computer is not simply a faster version of the laptop sitting on your desk. Its advantages depend on the type of problem it is trying to solve. Unfortunately for the cryptocurrency industry, some of those problems underpin the security of digital wallets. As explained in NewsBTC’s guide to quantum computing, blockchains rely on cryptographic signatures to establish ownership and authorize transactions. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could undermine some of the signature systems currently used to protect digital assets. How Could Quantum Computers Steal Cryptocurrency? When you send Bitcoin from your wallet, the network needs to establish that you have the authority to spend those coins. It does this by verifying a digital signature produced using your private key. Your private key is supposed to remain secret. The corresponding public key can be disclosed because working backward from a public key to its private counterpart is computationally impractical using conventional methods. Quantum computing could change that. In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor introduced a quantum algorithm that could efficiently solve certain mathematical problems underlying modern public-key cryptography. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running such an algorithm could potentially recover private keys from exposed public keys. An attacker could then create a transaction that the blockchain would recognize as valid, even though the original owner had never authorized it. That is a particularly uncomfortable problem for cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin does not have a customer service department that can reverse an unauthorized transfer. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has already developed alternative cryptographic standards intended to withstand these future attacks. The challenge for crypto is incorporating such protection into networks that were originally built around different assumptions. How Much Bitcoin Is Exposed to Quantum Computing? Bitcoin’s public transaction history makes it possible to estimate how much of its supply could be exposed under certain quantum attack scenarios. According to a November 25 snapshot from The Quantum Ledger, approximately 7.23 million BTC, representing 35.9% of issued supply under its methodology, was associated with public keys or spending scripts already visible on the blockchain. Around 1.94 million BTC was classified as exposed because of its output design. A further 5.29 million BTC was associated with addresses that had previously revealed relevant spending information. Some of these coins date back to Bitcoin’s earliest years, when transactions commonly revealed public keys directly. Estimates vary between researchers because they do not all measure exposure in exactly the same way. In May 2026, Glassnode’s research identified 6.04 million BTC under its own classification framework. These figures should not be interpreted as the amount of Bitcoin that will eventually be stolen. They measure a potential vulnerability under a specific future scenario, not an active attack. Owners of many exposed coins could migrate their holdings if suitable protection becomes available. Dormant wallets whose owners have lost their private keys present a considerably harder problem. Why Zcash Developers Want to Retire an Older Privacy System Zcash offers a useful example of how complicated a cryptographic migration can become. Unlike Bitcoin, where transactions are generally visible on a public ledger, Zcash provides privacy features through shielded pools. These allow users to transact without publicly revealing certain transaction details. Sapling is one of the network’s older shielded systems. Its proof mechanism relies on mathematical assumptions that Zakura believes warrant additional scrutiny in light of potentially accelerating cryptographic research. “ The time to prepare for a cryptographic breakthrough is before it happens. Zakura · Sapling retirement proposal Zakura proposed preventing new deposits into Sapling while encouraging users to migrate to Ironwood, a newer privacy system. If credible evidence of a threat emerged, further emergency measures could be considered. The amount involved is already changing. A November 27 snapshot from the Zcash Dashboard, timestamped 06:06 UTC, showed approximately 306,684 ZEC remaining in Sapling, below the rounded estimate cited in Zakura’s proposal. The difference does not, by itself, establish that the warning prompted users to move their funds. The discussion follows Zcash’s recent NU7 network upgrade, which improved transaction speed and continued the network’s transition away from older infrastructure. Importantly, the immediate concern raised by Zakura is not evidence of a successful quantum attack. It relates to speculative advances in mathematics that could affect particular cryptographic constructions. Those advances remain unverified. Can Zcash Become Quantum-Resistant? On November 25, Shielded Labs published an update on its Epoch project, which aims to develop privacy technology capable of withstanding future quantum computers. One of the problems its researchers are working on is the size of cryptographic proofs. Stronger protection can require considerably more data to be processed and transmitted. That can create difficulties for blockchains, where transaction capacity, verification costs and storage requirements already matter. The team is evaluating two possible approaches and expects to select a direction by the end of January 2027, provided its research progresses as planned. Ironwood already incorporates features intended to support a future recovery mechanism. However, the developers have made clear that these features do not make Zcash fully quantum-resistant today. The distinction is important. Having a contingency plan for a future attack is not the same as having protection against one. Are Bitcoin and Ethereum Preparing for Quantum Computing? Zcash is not the only network confronting these issues. Bitcoin developers are discussing changes through proposals including BIP-360, which would introduce a transaction output format designed to reduce certain forms of public-key exposure. A separate draft, BIP-361, explores a gradual transition away from vulnerable signature schemes once suitable alternatives are available. Neither proposal should be confused with an activated Bitcoin upgrade. Ethereum faces additional complications. Beyond individual wallets, its security model relies on cryptographic signatures used by validators and other infrastructure. Ethereum’s quantum-security challenge extends to staking arrangements and institutional custody. There is also a governance problem that applies particularly to Bitcoin. If millions of coins remain in old wallets that cannot be migrated, should the network eventually restrict their movement to prevent potential theft? Doing so could protect the broader ecosystem, but it could also prevent legitimate owners from accessing their own money. Leaving those coins untouched carries a different set of risks. Cryptography alone cannot settle that argument. When Will Quantum Computing Become a Real Threat to Crypto? There is no reliable date for when a quantum computer capable of breaking widely used cryptocurrency signatures will become available. Building such a machine requires more than increasing the number of qubits. Those qubits must also be reliable enough to carry out lengthy, complex calculations without errors overwhelming the results. According to Coinbase Institute’s research, the relevant machines do not yet exist, but the process of upgrading blockchains, wallets and custody infrastructure could itself take years. For that reason, waiting for an actual attack before implementing stronger cryptography would be a risky approach. Crypto investors should pay attention to what developers implement, whether wallets support the new protections and whether existing funds can be migrated without compromising ownership. There is no need to buy a token simply because its developers describe it as quantum-resistant, either. Such claims deserve scrutiny of the underlying cryptography and its implementation. Zcash’s latest proposals offer a glimpse of the decisions other blockchain communities may eventually face. Replacing an algorithm is one thing. Persuading an entire decentralized financial network to move its money before a deadline is something else entirely.
content: Zcash developers are pushing to retire older privacy systems and develop quantum-resistant technology amid concerns over future cryptographic threats. Meanwhile, researchers are analyzing how quantum computing could potentially expose public keys on networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum. While no quantum computer capable of breaking crypto signatures currently exists, upgrading blockchain infrastructure could take years, prompting early preparations across the industry.

title: Injective asks SEC to allow order books for tokenized stock trading

title: Visa and NBX to Make Stablecoins Easier to Use for Everyday Spending
summary:
Visa, a world leader in digital payments, NBX, Tieto and IDT Finance today announced plans for a new Visa Flex Card that will give eligible NBX customers a simpler way to use the different forms of money they hold.
Today, traditional currency and stablecoins typically sit in separate accounts and wallets. With the new card, expected to launch in 2027, customers have access to functionality that enables them to choose which eligible balance they want to use when they pay, without needing different cards or payment experiences.
Powered by Visa Flexible Credential, customers will be able to set their own preferences for how they want to pay. For example, they could use their local currency balance for everyday purchases and an eligible US dollar balance when paying in dollars, all through the same card. This may also reduce the need for currency conversions.
“We came from digital assets, and we want to make them useful in everyday life” said Stig Aleksander Kjos-Mathisen, CEO at NBX. “Visa Flexible Credential will make the money our customers hold more accessible, whether that’s traditional currency or a supported stablecoin, giving them a simple and familiar way to use it for everyday spending.”
“By embedding Visa Flex into our trusted, scalable card platform we are providing NBX with modern digital banking payment and stablecoin-related services”, says Aslak Lid, VP and Head of Cards at Tieto Banktech.
“People increasingly hold money in different forms and currencies, but using it should still be simple,” said Mathieu Altwegg, Head of Product & Solutions, Europe, Visa. “Visa Flexible Credential gives consumers more choice in how they pay, through one familiar credential. Working with NBX, we’re showing how stablecoins can move beyond something people hold to something they can use in everyday life.”
The NBX Visa Flex Card has the capability to enable eligible cardholders to:
Access supported traditional currency and stablecoin balances through one Visa card
Choose how they want to pay by setting preferences across eligible balances
Use the balance that best suits a purchase, including a matching currency balance where available
Over time, access additional funding sources, including traditional credit, through the same Visa credential
The collaboration brings together Visa's global payments network, NBX's digital asset expertise, Tieto's card and processing technology, and IDT Finance's issuing capabilities. The card is expected to initially launch with debit functionality across Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Germany, with plans to expand to Poland at a future date. Over time, NBX will leverage Visa Flexible Credential to add new funding sources, including traditional credit, to the same credential, giving customers greater choice over how they pay without needing a separate card.

Papa John's and TrueLayer have partnered with Lloyds to demonstrate how a checkout agent can incorporate Pay by Bank for a seamless agentic payment experience. 
Papa John’s AI agent helps the customer with their order, and then pays straight from the bank account the customer has linked to their Papa John’s account. Linking a bank account, rather than a card, is made possible by open banking technology, and this is the first time it has been combined with AI. When linking their account, the customer sets a spending limit with their bank, which cannot be exceeded by any AI agent - an inbuilt guardrail for the consumer. Authorisation happens within the user's bank app, so no credentials or passwords are ever shared with the agent.
TrueLayer, Europe’s leading Pay by Bank network, conducted a pilot with Papa John's that saw an AI agent complete a Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer for the first time. It also marked the first use of Lloyd’s variable recurring payment APIs for agentic payments. Conducted through the FCA’s Supercharged Sandbox, the work culminated in TrueLayer sharing its findings and learnings with the FCA and industry at the regulator’s showcase on 26 November.
AI agents are expected to handle a growing share of online shopping. TrueLayer is demonstrating that non-card payments can help maintain competition in payment acceptance in the age of AI commerce, and are better suited to agentic payments because consumers can set up mandates with their banks without sharing card details.
The customer sets up the mandate once, choosing their own spending limits per merchant or over specific time periods. The bank checks every payment against the customer's limits and declines anything above it. The customer can cancel the mandate with their merchant or from their banking app at any time.
Francesco Simoneschi, CEO and co-founder, TrueLayer: "Personal agents are changing the way we shop, and agentic commerce will be more disruptive than eCommerce was in 2000. Consumers want a safe, simple way for their agents to buy on their behalf. Merchants want to keep control of the customer experience while cutting cost and risk. And agents will choose the payment rail that is fastest, most secure and lowest cost, not the one people use out of habit. That's Pay by Bank: instant, secure, and governed by a digital mandate, with spending limits the customer sets with their own bank. Today it's pizza. Tomorrow it's everything else.”
This showcase demonstrates the potential for Open Banking technology to support agentic payments, which informs the work to create the right conditions and standards needed to adopt this technology fully and safely at scale

title: Asda Renews ClearScore Everywhere Partnership With New Three-Year Contract
summary:
ClearScore, the global data-driven financial services platform, today announces that Asda has renewed its partnership with ClearScore Everywhere for a further three years. The agreement extends an established relationship in which ClearScore Everywhere powers Asda Money’s loans marketplace.
The partnership has delivered almost 50% year-on-year growth in completed loans. The renewal will see ClearScore Everywhere continue to help Asda Money customers make more informed borrowing decisions by providing access to personalised loan options, powered by ClearScore's credit-matching technology and extensive network of lender partners, while helping Asda Money further develop its customer proposition.
ClearScore Everywhere is ClearScore's embedded credit marketplace platform, enabling retailers, financial services providers and comparison brands to integrate credit eligibility checks and personalised product matching into their own digital journeys. It powers Asda Money's loans marketplace, where customers can check their eligibility and compare options, helping them understand which loans may be available before applying.
Julia McColl, General Manager at ClearScore Everywhere, said:
“We’ve built a strong working relationship with the Asda Money team, helping them improve engagement and performance across credit products with our credit-matching technology and lender relationships.
“This three-year renewal allows us to build on this success; helping more Asda Money customers better understand their borrowing options and find financial products suited to their individual circumstances, empowering them to make more informed financial decisions.”
Samantha Inger, Head of Payments at Asda Money, said:
“We want to make it easier for our customers to access financial products that meet their needs, alongside the value they already expect from when they shop with Asda.
“Our partnership with ClearScore Everywhere helps customers better understand their options and compare loan products with confidence before they apply. Renewing the partnership for a further three years means we can continue making it simpler for customers to make informed decisions and access products that are right for them.”
